chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Muhammad ibn Rashid who said: Hisham ibn Ibrahim narrated to me that he
complained to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) of his illness and that no children were born to him. So he (the Imam) commanded him to raise his voice with the adhan in his house.
He (Hisham) said: So I did it, and God removed my illness from me, and my children became abundant.

Muhammad ibn Rashid said: I was perpetually afflicted with illness, never free from it — myself, a group of my servants, and my family — to the extent that I used to remain alone with no one to serve me. So when I heard that from Hisham, I acted upon it. And God removed the illnesses from me and from my family. And all praise is due to God.

key_terms.الْأَذَان: The adhan (call to prayer) — here recommended as a home practice for healing and blessing
key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ: All praise is due to God — closing expression of gratitude

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic practice of reciting the adhan at home for healing and seeking children?
ai.summary: This hadith recounts how Imam Abu al-Hasan (likely al-Ridha, AS) prescribed the practice of raising one's voice with the adhan inside the home as a remedy for chronic illness and childlessness. The narrator Hisham ibn Ibrahim experienced a miraculous cure after following this instruction, and Muhammad ibn Rashid corroborates the hadith by sharing his own parallel experience of healing for himself and his entire household. The hadith belongs to a section of al-Kafi dedicated to supplications and practices for seeking children, highlighting the Shia tradition of seeking blessings through specific acts of worship recommended by the Imams.
